第 63 章 Own the Narrative掌握叙事

Adam Baratz / 亚当·巴拉茨

— 第 181 页 —

"My PM doesn't understand why this project is so hard." "My team doesn't get any of the good projects." "Our architecture will collapse within six months." "Carryover is a fact of life on this team." "We need to replatform to survive peak." "We're making the right investments to survive peak." "My tech lead has me over-engineer everything."

「我的 PM 不理解为什么这个项目这么难。」「我的团队拿不到好项目。」「我们的架构六个月内会崩溃。」「遗留工作量是这个团队的生活现实。」「我们需要换平台才能撑过高峰。」「我们在做正确的投资来撑过高峰。」「我的技术领导让我把一切都过度工程化。」

A team is a cacophony of stories. You'll hear them at obvious times, like during a project kickoff. You'll hear them as asides in one-on-ones, glossed over without explanation because they're so "obvious" to the teller. You'll hear them as jokes in sprint planning sessions, poking fun at tensions between team members. You'll hear them as people get ready to start a meeting, in standup updates, in email, around the coffee machine. People share stories pretty much whenever they get together.

一个团队是故事的杂音。你会在明显的时候听到它们，比如项目启动时。你会在一对一中听到作为题外话，因为对讲述者太「明显」而不加解释地带过。你会在 sprint 计划会上听到作为笑话，取笑团队成员之间的紧张。你会在人们准备开始会议时、在站会更新中、在邮件中、在咖啡机旁听到。人们几乎聚在一起就分享故事。

Stories don't appear fully formed. They emerge as people draw connections between evidence. Imagine a stakeholder with limited visibility into the activities of a team. They might find the work that they request is frequently delayed and then abruptly deprioritized. They might not think much of it the first time. When it becomes a pattern, the stakeholder begins talking about how the team is unreliable and underperforming. The team's tech lead might tell an entirely different story. They eagerly jump on projects, but have trouble hitting estimates. Over multiple sprint retros, they identify a neglected system that is impeding a range of work streams. Rather than continue to struggle, they decide to pause feature work for a sprint so that they can shore up the neglected system. To the tech lead, this is another great example of how their team learns from problems and strengthens its ability to deliver.

故事不是完整成形出现的。它们在人们把证据之间建立联系时浮现。想象一个对团队活动可见度有限的利益相关者。他们可能发现他们要求的工作经常被延迟然后突然被降优先级。第一次可能没多想。当它变成模式，利益相关者开始谈论团队多不可靠、表现多差。团队的技术领导可能讲一个完全不同的故事。他们热切地跳上项目，但难以达到估算。在多次 sprint 回顾中，他们识别出一个被忽视的系统正在阻碍一系列工作流。他们没有继续挣扎，而是决定暂停功能开发一个 sprint，好加固那个被忽视的系统。对技术领导来说，这又是一个好例子说明他们团队怎么从问题中学习并加强交付能力。

— 第 182 页 —

Stories are typically incomplete, but rarely wrong. A story like that stakeholder's can be frustrating to hear as a manager. You likely have a more balanced and nuanced view of your team. Yet others are now acquiring a negative perception of them and becoming less willing to trust them with important work. Thankfully, as managers, we're uniquely positioned to shape the stories that people tell. Our roles usually ensure that we get face time with a large cross-section of an organization. Use that time to share the evidence that speaks to the breadth of what your team is engaging with. Don't stop there. Connect the dots and draw your audience to the stories that you want them to be telling.

故事通常不完整，但很少错。作为经理听到像那个利益相关者的故事会令人沮丧。你可能对团队有更平衡和细致的看法。然而其他人现在对他们形成负面看法，越来越不愿信任他们做重要工作。谢天谢地，作为经理，我们处于塑造人们讲述的故事的独特位置。我们的角色通常确保我们和组织的一大群人面对面交流。用那段时间分享能说明你团队参与广度的证据。不要停在那里。连点成线，把你的听众引导到你想让他们讲的故事。

Repetition is an important tool for spreading stories. Call out complementary groupings of evidence. Take every opportunity to retell a story. Maybe you've been impressing upon a team that it should get in control of the operational aspects of its system. Maybe an engineer says in a standup that they fixed a chronic issue after digging into some confusing log messages. Pull this piece of evidence into the broader story you're trying to tell: "I'm glad we're taking the time to get in control of the operational aspects of our system."

重复是传播故事的重要工具。指出互补的证据组合。抓住每个机会重述故事。也许你一直在让团队深刻认识到应该掌控系统的运维方面。也许一个工程师在站会上说他们在钻研一些令人困惑的日志消息后修复了一个长期问题。把这块证据拉进你想讲的更宽故事：「我很高兴我们在花时间掌控我们系统的运维方面。」

It's a good sign when people are nodding along and signaling familiarity with a story. It means the story is no longer background noise. They're consciously using it to assess the world around them. It's a better sign when you hear people repeating stories you tell. It means a story has resonated at a deeper level, that it has become a tool for achieving their goals. People are now tracking to your direction without you having to stand over their shoulders.

当人们点头表示熟悉一个故事时是好迹象。它意味着故事不再是背景噪音。他们有意识地用它评估周围世界。当你听到人们重复你讲的故事时是更好的迹象。它意味着一个故事在更深层次共鸣，它已成为实现目标的工具。人们现在朝你的方向走，不用你站在他们肩膀上盯着。

When negative stories spread, they give you an opportunity to connect with your audience. Oftentimes, all you need to do is ask. Someone who is telling others that they're frustrated with your team would likely welcome the opportunity to tell you why they're frustrated. Ask questions to understand their evidence. This will help you understand their values. A stakeholder who sees a team as unreliable is telling you what he thinks reliability looks like. He could be telling you how he values the different capabilities of your team, potentially that he doesn't know how to place a value on some of them. He could be telling you where he gets his evidence and how information flows through an organization. These kinds of conversations are opportunities to win over detractors, but you should also be open to changing your mind about a situation. You could find that you're misaligned with an organization's objectives and that you need to retune. You want to be telling the best stories. Make them stick. Own the narrative.

当负面故事传播时，它们给你和听众连接的机会。通常，你只需要问。一个告诉别人对你团队失望的人很可能欢迎机会告诉你他们为什么失望。问问题理解他们的证据。这会帮你理解他们的价值观。一个把团队看作不可靠的利益相关者在告诉你他认为可靠是什么样。他可能在告诉你他怎么评价你团队的不同能力，可能他不知道怎么给其中一些估值。他可能在告诉你他从哪里得到证据、信息怎么在组织中流动。这类对话是赢得批评者的机会，但你也应该对改变对情况的看法持开放态度。你可能发现你和组织目标不对齐，需要重新调整。你想讲最好的故事。让它们扎根。掌握叙事。
